equations.title: Earth-fed orbital deployment
equations.interpretation: Commissioned orbital compute rises with delivered launch service and falls with depreciation. With a fixed delivery rate, this is a bounded deployment process rather than self-compounding industrial growth.
operators: The time derivative is the instantaneous change in commissioned capacity.
assumptions: Delivery productivity and depreciation are held fixed in the illustrative steady-state reading.
equations.implementationStatus: Analytical comparison; the integrated model represents deployment with explicit annual flows.

equations.title: Endogenous hardware growth
equations.interpretation: Installed productive hardware compounds only when its gross reproduction rate exceeds its loss rate. The equation isolates the closure condition and does not imply that either rate stays constant in a real industrial system.
operators: The derivative reports net hardware-capacity change per unit time.
assumptions: The displayed exponential form is an idealized local approximation with aggregate rates.
equations.implementationStatus: Conceptual benchmark; the sector model uses constrained, time-varying reproduction and loss.

equations.title: Coupled RSI causal system
equations.interpretation: Intelligence, task-level autonomy, productive capacity, and usable compute form a delayed four-stage causal loop. Resource states, depreciation, saturation, construction, commissioning, verification, and authorization prevent an unconstrained or instantaneous conversion between stages.
operators: The projection operators impose declared ceilings; elementwise products apply sector-specific loss and gate vectors; each response function is saturating and resource bounded. The local elasticity product or Jacobian spectral radius diagnoses only perturbation amplification near one state.
assumptions: The compact system summarizes separately implemented model layers. Local gain above one is neither physical closure nor a guarantee of global growth, stability, safety, or indefinite improvement.
equations.implementationStatus: Operationalized across the digital, industrial, compute, and governance modules.

equations.title: Internal capability update and public release mapping
equations.interpretation: A candidate enters internally available capability only after technical validation and authorization for its bounded internal role. Publicly observable capability is a separately authorized, potentially lagged, narrowed, or differently optimized release mapping of an internal state.
indices: n indexes candidate-improvement attempts; r indexes public-release events; tau maps a release to the internal state it exposes.
operators: Bold symbols are vectors; multiplication by the technical and internal binary gates suppresses invalid or unauthorized internal updates; the release operator need not preserve every capability component.
assumptions: Capability components retain declared scales rather than being collapsed into one universal intelligence scalar.
The conceptual release mapping does not impose universal componentwise nesting; the implemented three sensitivity cases use nested public slices and label the resulting gap as assumption-class.
equations.implementationStatus: The vector relation is conceptual; the implemented scalar projection tracks experiment, technical-validation, internal-adoption, and public-release clocks separately.

equations.title: Diminishing-return capability frontier
equations.interpretation: Capability increases with cumulative effective effort while its marginal gain declines toward a fixed-regime ceiling. The curve is a sensitivity family, not an empirical law of recursive improvement.
indices: m identifies a held-out capability component.
operators: The first and second derivative signs impose positive but diminishing marginal response.
assumptions: The attainable improvement, scale, and curvature are scenario parameters and the regime is held fixed.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as a bounded sensitivity option and compared with alternative progress regimes.

equations.title: Effective training compute
equations.interpretation: Physical training work is converted to task-relevant effective compute by separate hardware, utilization, algorithmic, and architecture factors. Sparse and dense models therefore need not obtain the same useful effort from the same nominal FLOP.
operators: The approximate equality is an operation-count model, not an exact hardware measurement.
assumptions: Every efficiency ratio must name a baseline and a matched held-out target.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the digital-progress sensitivity and reported by component.

equations.title: AI-R&D compute allocation
equations.interpretation: A conserved accelerator-hour budget is split across research uses, and verified progress is limited by the slowest researcher, experiment, data, verification, or serial-time stage. More model copies cannot bypass a physical or verification bottleneck.
indices: s indexes compute uses in the allocation set.
operators: Each minimum selects the binding capacity; the sum enforces conservation of physical accelerator hours.
assumptions: Conversion efficiencies and per-candidate compute costs are scenario inputs with compatible units.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the integrated digital-loop allocation analysis.

equations.title: Chronological release backtest
equations.interpretation: Chance-adjusted benchmark performance is fitted to training-compute scale and distance from a declared compute-optimal token allocation. The chronology separates training, validation, and holdout releases.
indices: i indexes publicly released models in chronological order.
operators: logit maps a probability to log odds; the minimum makes the balance score symmetric around the target token-to-parameter ratio.
assumptions: The small historical sample supports a diagnostic backtest, not a universal scaling law.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as a reproducible historical fit with held-out release checks.

equations.title: Verified-loop bottleneck
equations.interpretation: End-to-end improvement throughput equals the capacity of the slowest required stage. Training speed alone cannot determine loop speed when data, experiments, evaluation, safety, deployment, or observation bind.
operators: The minimum selects the binding serial stage.
assumptions: All stage rates are measured in completed-loop equivalents per year over the same boundary.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as the digital-loop throughput bottleneck.

equations.title: Capability gain rate
equations.interpretation: Capability changes at verified-loop throughput multiplied by the conditional expected gain of a successful loop. Because the expected gain depends on current state and evidence, the relation does not assume constant progress per loop.
indices: n identifies the candidate loop whose conditional gain distribution is evaluated.
operators: The expectation averages gain conditional on the current capability, data, architecture, compute, and verification state.
assumptions: Loop throughput and conditional gain use compatible time and capability units.
equations.implementationStatus: Operationalized by the discrete intelligence update in Appendix D.

equations.title: Independent verification throughput
equations.interpretation: Candidate throughput is reduced by acceptance yield, false positives, and evaluator dependence, then capped by direction-setting and execution capacity. This keeps producing candidates distinct from licensing verified progress.
indices: k indexes verification classes with different evidence requirements.
operators: Minimum operators select the binding verification and licensing capacities.
assumptions: Yield, false-positive, and independence factors are bounded fractions measured for each class.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the verification-hierarchy sensitivity.

equations.title: Accepted training signal
equations.interpretation: Useful training signal is the portion of synthetic and physical records that survives deduplication, filtering, provenance, evaluator-error, diversity, and causal-linkage losses. Raw data volume is therefore not treated as learning value.
indices: g indexes successive learning generations.
operators: Multiplicative fractions act as sequential acceptance filters; the two additive terms distinguish synthetic and physical evidence.
assumptions: All record counts are converted to the same accepted-signal unit before addition.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the data/evaluator co-evolution scenarios.

equations.title: Authorized capacity throughput
equations.interpretation: New authorized capacity cannot exceed the slowest applicable reliability, adversarial, command, environmental, treaty, or human-authorization channel. Any gross capacity beyond that cumulative authorization account is reported separately as unauthorized.
operators: The minimum is a rate constraint; the positive-part gross addition excludes retirement from proposed additions.
assumptions: Only controls applicable to the scenario boundary enter the minimum, with all channels converted to authorization actions per year.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the authorized-capacity control trajectory.

equations.title: Marginal response to intelligence
equations.interpretation: The finite-difference quotient measures how much a regime's terminal operating capacity changes under a declared capability perturbation while complementary stocks and gates are held fixed. It is a local scenario diagnostic, not a price or universal production coefficient.
indices: r indexes the modeled industrial regime.
operators: The quotient is a finite difference rather than an infinitesimal derivative.
assumptions: The perturbation is positive and all components of the complementary-state vector remain fixed.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as a two-sided scenario comparison over declared perturbations.

equations.title: Embodiment adequacy gate
equations.interpretation: Hardware is adequate for a task only if every required sensing, actuation, latency, safety, and process dimension clears its threshold. Greater intelligence cannot compensate for a physically impossible or unobservable task interface.
indices: k indexes tasks; p indexes the task's hard embodiment dimensions.
operators: The indicator is one when a threshold passes, and the product implements an all-required logical AND.
assumptions: Each dimension is oriented so that a larger signed adequacy margin is better.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the task–embodiment compatibility sweep.

equations.title: Intelligence–embodiment compatibility
equations.interpretation: Conditional on adequate hardware, task success rises sigmoidally with sufficiently high intelligence toward an embodiment-specific ceiling. If the hardware gate fails, the attainable success score remains zero regardless of intelligence.
indices: k indexes a task–embodiment pair.
operators: The logistic term is a bounded S-curve; multiplication by the adequacy gate enforces the physical prerequisite.
assumptions: The sigmoid location and slope are assumption-class sensitivity parameters, not measured universal constants.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as a bounded two-direction sensitivity surface.

equations.title: Embodied-task first passage
equations.interpretation: The first threshold identifies the minimum intelligence that can reach the required task score with the available hardware. The second gives the first time both that intelligence and independent verification are present, which may be never within the modeled horizon.
indices: k indexes a task–embodiment pair.
operators: The infimum selects the earliest or smallest value satisfying the condition; logical AND requires capability and verification together.
assumptions: If no feasible value exists, the threshold is infinite rather than missing.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as a threshold and first-passage diagnostic.

equations.title: Data-advantage profile
equations.interpretation: Data advantage is represented first as seven separately auditable dimensions. Any aggregate score is a declared mapping from that profile and cannot conceal the underlying evidence and uncertainty.
indices: j indexes the seven data-advantage dimensions.
operators: Bold d is a vector; F is an explicitly chosen scalarization, not an empirically fixed law.
assumptions: Every component is normalized to a common direction and accompanied by an uncertainty interval and evidence class.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as a reported component profile plus optional scalar sensitivity.

equations.title: Gated data-advantage scalar
equations.interpretation: Access, causal linkage, and verification must clear hard floors before a weighted geometric mean can summarize the profile. The construction prevents a strong component from numerically compensating for a failed prerequisite.
indices: j indexes data dimensions included in the aggregate.
operators: Indicators enforce hard gates; the weighted geometric mean is zero if an included component is zero.
assumptions: Weights, thresholds, and missing-data treatment are scenario choices with no claimed empirical calibration.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented only as an assumption-class sensitivity; the full profile remains primary.

equations.title: Matched lifecycle cost
equations.interpretation: Each environment is charged for the same lifecycle categories, including internal opportunity costs and terminal residual value, over a common functional unit and horizon. The ratio and difference expose relative and absolute cost gaps.
indices: e indexes environment; k indexes matched lifecycle categories.
operators: Present value discounts dated flows; the category sum enforces the matched accounting boundary.
assumptions: Currency year, functional unit, horizon, discounting, and system boundary are identical across the compared environments.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the lifecycle-cost decomposition and Monte Carlo comparison.

equations.title: Centrifugal acceleration
equations.interpretation: Radial acceleration grows with rotor radius and the square of angular speed. The relation converts a process acceleration requirement into a mechanical design constraint, not a claim that an entire facility needs artificial gravity.
assumptions: The expression assumes uniform circular motion at the stated radius.
equations.implementationStatus: Used to derive process-specific centrifuge penalties.

equations.title: Net hardware growth
equations.interpretation: Hardware expands when gross replication exceeds aggregate depreciation and contracts when losses dominate. The simple law is a diagnostic benchmark; repair, recycling, obsolescence, and logistics are modeled separately downstream.
operators: The derivative is the instantaneous net change in installed productive capacity.
assumptions: Aggregate reproduction and depreciation rates summarize heterogeneous sectors only for this conceptual comparison.
equations.implementationStatus: Replaced operationally by the multisector stock-and-flow model.

equations.title: Depreciation decomposition
equations.interpretation: Total frontier-equivalent depreciation is separated into wear, catastrophic loss, obsolescence, and logistics loss. The decomposition keeps repair and recycling visible instead of hiding them inside a reduced loss rate.
assumptions: Components use a common capacity-equivalent rate and are additive over the declared reporting interval.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented per sector and environment.

equations.title: Orbital lifecycle state transition
equations.interpretation: Orbital assets move among operating, degraded, service, repair, recovery, waste, and debris states while deployments and removals enter through an external-flow vector. This makes repair and recycling explicit stock transitions.
indices: i and j index lifecycle states; t indexes discrete simulation time.
operators: Matrix transpose routes inflows; diag of outward rates subtracts departures from each state.
assumptions: Transition rates are nonnegative and the time step is small enough for the explicit update to preserve valid stocks.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the orbital lifecycle sensitivity.

equations.title: Effective irreversible loss
equations.interpretation: Irrecoverable waste and uncontrolled debris accumulated over the horizon are divided by operating-capacity-years. The diagnostic excludes recoverable failures and makes the residual loss burden comparable across scenarios.
operators: Time integrals accumulate irreversible losses and operating exposure over the declared horizon.
assumptions: Numerator and denominator use the same capacity-equivalent unit and the operating exposure is positive.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as a horizon-level lifecycle diagnostic.

equations.title: Orbital service decision value
equations.interpretation: A service action is worthwhile only when failure-adjusted preserved output, avoided launch, recovered asset value, upgrades, and residual value exceed variable, amortized, routing, downtime, risk, and depreciation costs.
indices: a indexes service action, o orbit, c asset class, and f service fleet.
operators: The failure complement discounts benefits; fixed fleet cost is amortized across annual clients and fleet life.
assumptions: All benefits and costs use real-2025 MUSD per client event and a common service boundary.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the orbital service decision comparison.

equations.title: Orbital common-cause loss budget
equations.interpretation: For every credible hazard set, the capacity simultaneously exposed to that event must stay below a declared fraction of total service capacity. The constraint turns cluster size and reserve distribution into design outputs.
indices: h indexes credible common-cause hazard sets; i indexes capacity nodes.
operators: The indicator includes a node in a hazard set; the maximum selects the worst credible event.
assumptions: The hazard-set inventory is complete for the declared environment and restoration window.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the cluster-layout and breakup-cloud strategy sweeps.

equations.title: Critical-component replenishment
equations.interpretation: Every critical component must be replenished before redundancy, spares, repair, and substitution cease to keep it available. A small mass fraction can therefore set the survival clock for the whole system.
indices: j indexes critical component classes.
operators: The strict inequality is a viability condition for every critical class.
assumptions: Effective survival includes inventory and recovery options rather than time to first failure.
equations.implementationStatus: Enforced through sector balances, stocks, imports, repair, and substitution.

equations.title: Net productive-capacity growth
equations.interpretation: Net growth is production minus losses, normalized by installed productive infrastructure. Zero separates sustaining the stock from expanding it.
assumptions: Production, losses, and stock are measured over a consistent period and capacity-equivalent boundary.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as sector and balanced-system growth diagnostics.

equations.title: Critical-input closure ratio
equations.interpretation: The ratio reports the share of critical inputs produced inside the modeled network. It is descriptive only: autonomy still depends on which residual inputs remain irreplaceable.
assumptions: The numerator and denominator use the same declared critical-input weighting.
equations.implementationStatus: Reported alongside process closure and residual import composition.

equations.title: Autonomy and import leverage
equations.interpretation: Strict autonomy requires zero external flow for every critical input, while support intensity and its inverse quantify how much outside mass unlocks verified capacity. Partial closure can greatly reduce entry capital without being mislabeled self-sufficiency.
indices: j indexes critical external input classes.
operators: The product of indicators implements all-critical-input autonomy; the inverse is undefined when external flow is zero.
assumptions: External mass flows and verified capacity additions share a declared annual accounting boundary.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the partial-closure dashboard and supplier-boundary analysis.

equations.title: Externally supported capacity update
equations.interpretation: Sector capacity changes through locally produced additions, imported-input-enabled additions, and elementwise depreciation. The equation represents hybrid expansion explicitly rather than treating partial closure as autonomy.
indices: Vector components index modeled industrial sectors.
operators: The Hadamard product applies each sector's loss rate to its own capacity.
assumptions: Local and imported additions are commissioned within the same discrete-step convention.
equations.implementationStatus: Operationalized by the multisector material, service, and import constraints.

equations.title: Coordination workload
equations.interpretation: Coordination work rises with active task-graph edges, complexity, and uncertainty, while coordination-relevant intelligence compresses only the reducible portion. An irreducible sensing, latency, safety, and verification floor remains.
operators: Power-law elasticities control sensitivity around named reference values; the denominator produces bounded reduction toward the floor.
assumptions: This is an assumption-class sensitivity form and all normalized ratios are positive.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in coordination-form and uncertainty sensitivity tables.

equations.title: Commissioned bottleneck upgrade
equations.interpretation: A proposed bottleneck upgrade contributes capacity only after design, construction, and verification lags and only when budget, producing-sector, and causal-verification gates pass. Intelligence can improve proposals without making unbuilt hardware available.
indices: p indexes candidate bottleneck-upgrade projects.
operators: Indicator products implement simultaneous time, budget, production, and verification gates.
assumptions: Physical floors and unavailable external decisions set the proposed increment to zero.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the bottleneck-project trajectory.

equations.title: Irreducible coordination burden
equations.interpretation: The coordination floor is the sum of sensing, latency, synchronization, safety, verification, and contention burdens. Some terms can vanish for isolated tasks, but intelligence alone does not erase physical observation or governance requirements.
assumptions: Unlike burdens are added only after explicit conversion to the common agent-hour-equivalent account.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as the irreducible floor in coordination sensitivities.

equations.title: Cognitive–physical labor bottleneck
equations.interpretation: Effective physical-agent capacity is limited by the scarcest model, compute, robot, sensor, safety, task, tool, or verification resource. Experiment duration also contains an irreducible serial term plus the number of parallel batches.
operators: The minimum selects the binding resource; the ceiling counts complete parallel experiment batches.
assumptions: All capacity terms count compatible simultaneously usable agent-equivalents.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the cognitive–physical labor sensitivity.

equations.title: Cumulative created hardware
equations.interpretation: Total hardware created by time t is the integral of productive throughput. The relation distinguishes cumulative production from the surviving installed stock.
operators: The integral accumulates instantaneous throughput over elapsed time.
assumptions: Throughput and created hardware share a consistent capacity-equivalent unit.
equations.implementationStatus: Reported from simulated production trajectories.

equations.title: Intelligence-coupled hardware growth
equations.interpretation: Gross reproduction can improve with intelligence, energy, and materials, but net hardware growth still subtracts depreciation and remains constrained by the weakest physical sector. The compact relation summarizes coupling rather than replacing the detailed allocator.
operators: The time derivative reports net change; the reproduction-rate function summarizes coupled inputs.
assumptions: The aggregate function hides sector bottlenecks and is used only as a conceptual envelope.
equations.implementationStatus: Operationalized by the ten-sector lexicographic allocator.

equations.title: Material balance
equations.interpretation: A material stock changes by recovered production, initial or external supply, and inbound transfers minus sector builds, losses, and outbound transfers. Every modeled element must balance across Earth, lunar, orbital, and asteroid arcs.
indices: e indexes material categories, s source/process routes, a transfer arcs, and j industrial sectors.
operators: The signed sums implement conservation within the declared system boundary.
assumptions: All flows are converted to the same material unit and interval; unmodeled chemical-species closure is not implied.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the seed optimizer and dynamic sector model.

equations.title: Annualized capital recovery
equations.interpretation: The capital-recovery factor converts up-front cost into an equivalent annual charge, while the space annualization factor adds operations and insurance and subtracts discounted residual value.
operators: Discounting uses compound annual rates over the declared service life.
assumptions: The discount rate and life are positive and all rate add-ons use annual fractions of installed capital.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the lifecycle-cost calculator.

equations.title: Space lifecycle cost
equations.interpretation: Annualized orbital service cost includes compute hardware, infrastructure, launch mass, regulatory flow, and delivered utilization. Its affine form separates launch-price-sensitive cost from the non-launch intercept.
operators: The affine decomposition groups all launch-independent terms into alpha and launch-mass exposure into beta.
assumptions: All costs are measured per delivered frontier-equivalent kilowatt-year with matched real-dollar and utilization conventions.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented for disposable and serviceable orbital architectures.

equations.title: Earth lifecycle cost
equations.interpretation: The terrestrial counterfactual annualizes accelerators and data-center infrastructure, adds electricity, adjusts for frontier-equivalent performance, and divides by utilization.
assumptions: The Earth and space cases use the same delivered-compute functional unit and currency year.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented with responsive frontier and older-node hardware cases.

equations.title: Launch-price break-even
equations.interpretation: The break-even launch price is the price at which affine space lifecycle cost equals the matched Earth cost. A negative result means non-launch space costs already exceed the terrestrial counterfactual.
assumptions: The launch-mass coefficient beta is positive and the affine cost boundary remains valid over the tested range.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented across orbital regimes and uncertainty draws.

equations.title: Central space-cost substitution
equations.interpretation: The central LEO serviceable-platform parameters are substituted into the space lifecycle equation to expose the arithmetic behind the reported annual cost.
assumptions: The displayed value uses the named central case and real-2025 USD per delivered kilowatt-year.
equations.implementationStatus: Generated from the same parameterized lifecycle-cost calculation used in the tables.

equations.title: Milestone control gate
equations.interpretation: A branch is control-admissible only if control readiness arrives no later than AI-R&D closure and both terrestrial and space industrial closure. Capability that outruns these controls is not counted as a successful endpoint.
operators: Each indicator tests one ordering condition; their product implements logical AND.
assumptions: Milestone times share the same baseline and operational definitions.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the milestone-order branch analysis.

equations.title: Replication governance gate
equations.interpretation: Productive capacity is split into authorized and unauthorized stocks, and a branch passes only when unauthorized and preemptive shares, legitimacy, externality internalization, and every governance gate meet declared thresholds.
indices: j indexes required governance gates.
operators: The outer indicator converts the conjunction of all endpoint conditions to a binary result.
assumptions: Thresholds and required gates are normative scenario inputs, not empirical constants.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in governance-externality and threat-control traceability analyses.

equations.title: Welfare-relevant activity accounts
equations.interpretation: Relocated harm, net expansion, humanitarian service, science, and industrial expansion are reported as separate activity coordinates. The vector deliberately avoids a scalar welfare total that would hide distribution and externalities.
operators: Bold A is a vector of distinct accounts, not a weighted sum.
assumptions: Normative weights, rights, consent, and distribution remain outside the engineering model.
equations.implementationStatus: Conceptual reporting framework; no aggregate welfare score is implemented.

equations.title: Appendix material balance
equations.interpretation: This specification-level identity restates the material conservation law used by the optimizer and dynamic model: inputs and transfers must cover builds, losses, exports, and stock change.
indices: e indexes material categories, s source/process routes, a transfer arcs, and j industrial sectors.
operators: Signed sums enforce conservation within the modeled system boundary.
assumptions: All flows use consistent units and the stated annual or horizon interval.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the seed optimizer and dynamic sector model.

equations.title: Task coverage by capability
equations.interpretation: Unscripted task coverage rises linearly with capability above the baseline until it reaches an embodiment- and process-specific ceiling. The relation is a sensitivity convention for residual intervention, not a measured universal automation curve.
indices: j indexes industrial processes.
operators: The inner maximum prevents below-baseline gains; the outer minimum enforces the coverage ceiling.
assumptions: Coverage is smoothly divisible in this approximation and can miss hard threshold tasks.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in sector productivity and intervention constraints.

equations.title: Process centrifuge speed
equations.interpretation: The required rotation rate supplies only the acceleration gap between a process requirement and lunar gravity, scaled by rotor radius. Processes needing no additional acceleration receive no centrifuge penalty.
indices: j indexes industrial processes.
operators: The maximum clips a negative acceleration gap to zero; the square root converts acceleration and radius to angular speed.
assumptions: Uniform circular motion and the declared effective rotor radius are used.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in process-specific mass and power penalties.

equations.title: Seed-mass objective
equations.interpretation: The optimizer minimizes initial digital hardware, effective sector build mass, and strategic material stocks while satisfying closure, throughput, task, lag, and intervention constraints.
indices: j indexes sectors and e material categories.
operators: Nested sums aggregate each sector's effective bill of materials and the initial strategic stocks.
assumptions: All objective components are expressed in transported seed mass under the declared system boundary.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as the linear-program objective.

equations.title: Implemented intelligence update
equations.interpretation: Capability gain per step is limited by verified-loop throughput, four effective-compute efficiencies, installed-compute signal, and a shrinking frontier factor, then capped at the declared regime maximum.
indices: t is elapsed simulation time; the update advances by Δt.
operators: The outer minimum caps capability; the logarithm gives diminishing compute response; the frontier factor shrinks as capability approaches its ceiling.
assumptions: This is a declared sensitivity law with normalized capability, not a validated universal intelligence-growth equation.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the integrated simulation and swept across learning regimes.

equations.title: Lexicographic balanced-growth stage
equations.interpretation: The first allocation stage maximizes the worst sector's net growth while respecting repair limits, service capacity, recycling yield, direct imports, and inventory withdrawals. No sector can be sacrificed to inflate aggregate output.
indices: j indexes productive sectors, i service sectors or inventories, and c depreciation components.
operators: For-all constraints enforce every sector and service balance; indicators activate repair and recycling terms only in their corresponding service rows.
assumptions: Coefficients, recovery fractions, and direct imports use compatible annual capacity units and nonnegative bounds.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented with HiGHS as stage one of the lexicographic allocation.

equations.title: Recoverable retirement
equations.interpretation: Recoverable retirement equals the recoverable share of each sector's component losses minus wear failures already diverted into repair. This prevents repaired capacity from also being counted as recycling feedstock.
indices: j indexes sectors and c depreciation components.
operators: The double sum aggregates recoverable component losses; the subtraction prevents double counting of repaired wear.
assumptions: Recovery shares are bounded fractions and use the same loss decomposition as sector depreciation.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented in the recycling-feed constraint.

equations.title: Normalized allocation tie-break
equations.interpretation: After preserving the growth and secondary optima, the final stage selects the unique smallest normalized action vector. State-derived scales prevent sectors with large numerical units from dominating the tie-break.
indices: j indexes sector actions and i inventory withdrawals.
operators: Squared normalized actions form a strictly convex norm, giving a unique solution on the retained optimal face.
assumptions: Every normalization scale is positive and protected by a numerical floor.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented with OSQP and a documented SLSQP fallback.

equations.title: Capacity and inventory updates
equations.interpretation: Sector capacity advances by build, repair, and depreciation flows with a small positive numerical floor. Inventories add inflow, subtract use and shelf-life loss, and remain clipped between zero and storage capacity.
indices: j indexes sectors and i inventories.
operators: max applies the numerical capacity floor; clip enforces the physical inventory interval.
assumptions: Flows are held constant within each explicit time step and use consistent annual units.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented after each lexicographic allocation step.

equations.title: Realized balanced growth
equations.interpretation: Realized system growth is the worst sector's post-shock fractional change over the step. It is reported separately from the allocator's pre-shock target so disruptions cannot disappear from the headline rate.
indices: j indexes productive sectors.
operators: The minimum selects the slowest sector after shocks.
assumptions: Pre-step capacities are positive and post-shock and pre-step states use the same capacity units.
equations.implementationStatus: Implemented as the reported balanced-growth diagnostic.
